**At Naval Academy graduation, Obama honors military—and former rival McCain’s son**

By CNN Staff  
Updated 4:15 PM EDT, Fri May 22, 2009

**ANNAPOLIS, Maryland (CNN) —** Just six months after one of the most fiercely fought presidential elections in recent memory, President Barack Obama and his former political rival, Sen. John McCain, found themselves united Friday in a stadium filled with navy blue and gold. 

Delivering his first commencement address as Commander-in-Chief to the U.S. Naval Academy, President Obama saluted the 1,034 newly commissioned officers—among them Ensign John S. "Jack" McCain IV, the son of the Arizona senator.

The moment underscored a stark transition from the partisan battlegrounds of 2008 to the shared traditions of military service, providing a poignant backdrop to the President's address on national security and foreign policy.

Addressing a packed audience at the Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium under a bright May sky, Obama directly acknowledged the deep legacy of service embodied by the McCain family. 

"We see it in the family of your classmate Jack McCain," Obama told the cheering crowd, as Sen. McCain and his wife, Cindy, watched from the stands. "Jack is the fourth generation of his family to serve. His father, Senator John McCain, is here today. And we are profoundly grateful to the McCain family for their generations of service to our nation."

The applause that followed served as a brief pause in national politics, highlighting a moment of personal reconciliation and mutual respect between the leader of the Democratic Party and the 2008 Republican presidential nominee. 

### A Legacy Continued

For the younger McCain, 22, the graduation marks his entry into a long family line of naval history. Both his father and grandfather, Admiral John S. "Jack" McCain Jr., graduated from the Academy, as did his great-grandfather, Admiral John S. "Slew" McCain Sr. 

Following the ceremony, Sen. McCain—himself a 1958 Naval Academy graduate and former prisoner of war in Vietnam—expressed quiet pride in his son’s accomplishment, steering clear of political commentary to focus entirely on his role as a father.

"Cindy and I are immensely proud of Jack and all the young men and women who graduated today," McCain said in a brief statement released after the event. "They represent the best of America."

President Obama stood on stage for hours, shaking the hand of every single graduate, including the younger McCain, offering a smile and words of encouragement as the newly minted ensign crossed the stage.

### 'Pragmatism and Principles'

In his main address, President Obama used the platform to outline his vision for the future of the American military, stressing that the nation must adapt to an increasingly complex world defined by unconventional threats, cyber warfare, and long wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.

"We will maintain America's military dominance," Obama declared, promising to keep the armed forces the best-trained and best-equipped in the world. However, he warned the fresh graduates that raw military power alone could not protect the country.

"You will be asked to lead in a world of swift and uncertain change," the President said. "In this new era, our security depends on a smart, pragmatic combination of all elements of American power."

Obama reiterated his commitment to upholding American values while pursuing national security, touching upon his administration’s decisions to end harsh interrogation techniques and work toward closing the detention facility at Guantanamo Bay—positions that Senator McCain has notably supported in the past, putting him at odds with some within his own party.

### A Tradition Sealed

As the speech concluded, the traditional cap toss filled the air above the stadium, a white cloud signaling the end of four years of rigorous training and the beginning of military service during a time of two ongoing foreign wars.

For the graduates, the day was about duty and country. But for the thousands looking on—and the millions watching nationwide—the sight of President Obama saluting John McCain's son served as a powerful reminder of the common bond that ties the nation’s leaders together, regardless of party lines.

"The uniform you wear today," Obama told the class of 2009, "belongs to no political party. It belongs to the United States of America."

Watching from the stands at Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium was his former political rival, Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.), who attended not as a politician, but as a proud father. Among the 1,034 midshipmen receiving their commissions was his son, John "Jack" S. McCain IV.

Addressing the stadium packed with over 30,000 spectators, President Obama emphasized the solemn duties awaiting the new officers in an era defined by twin wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and emerging global threats. He urged the graduates to maintain the highest standards of integrity and moral courage.

"We will uphold the ideals that we advance," Obama told the stadium. "We will maintain the discipline and accountability that sets the United States military apart."

The ceremony marked a poignant moment of post-election reconciliation. As President Obama took the podium, he acknowledged the McCain family's deep ties to Annapolis, drawing warm applause from the crowd and a nod from the Arizona senator in the audience. 

For the younger McCain, 22, the day was the culmination of four grueling years at the Academy and the continuation of a formidable family dynasty. Jack McCain represents the fourth generation of his family to graduate from the Naval Academy, following his great-grandfather, Admiral John S. McCain Sr.; his grandfather, Admiral John S. McCain Jr.; and his father, a former Navy pilot and Vietnam War prisoner of war.

Speaking to reporters following the ceremony, the newly commissioned Ensign Jack McCain reflected on the pressure and pride of carrying such a storied name. When asked about the personal guidance his father gave him to navigate both life and the rigors of military service, Jack shared a piece of quintessential McCain advice.

"My dad told me early on: 'Don't lie, cheat or steal -- anything else is fair game,'" Jack said with a grin, recalling the practical wisdom handed down by his father. 

While the family legacy looms large, the younger McCain was eager to forge his own path. Set to report to flight school in Pensacola, Florida, to train as a Navy helicopter pilot, Jack noted that his time at the Academy was about proving himself on his own merits. 

Senator McCain, who graduated near the bottom of his own Annapolis class in 1958, expressed immense pride in his son's achievement, noting with a smile that Jack had managed to finish significantly higher in the class rankings than he ever did.

As the ceremony concluded with the traditional midshipmen cap toss, sending hundreds of white covers soaring into the Maryland sky, the focus shifted from political rivalries to the shared sacrifice of the nation's newest military leaders. 

For President Obama and the McCain family, the day served as a vivid reminder of the common bond of service that unites the country above political divides. As Ensign Jack McCain joined his classmates in celebrating their new officer rank, he stepped directly into the nation's service—armed with a historic legacy and his father's simple rules to live by.

**ANNAPOLIS, Md.** — In his first commencement address to a military academy as Commander-in-Chief, President Barack Obama told the United States Naval Academy’s Class of 2009 on Friday that America’s national security relies as much on its moral values and international alliances as it does on its military power.

Speaking under bright skies before a crowd of over 30,000 at the Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium, Obama addressed 1,036 newly commissioned Navy ensigns and Marine Corps second lieutenants. The President used the platform to outline a vision of national defense rooted in pragmatism, adherence to American principles, and a commitment to moral leadership.

"Our moral leadership does not come from claiming that our values are universal, but by acting on them at home and abroad," Obama told the graduates. "We will uphold our standards and our ideals. We will reject torture, and we will respect the rule of law."

The speech came at a pivotal moment in American foreign policy. The nation was engaged in two ongoing wars, with the administration actively planning a withdrawal from Iraq while shifting greater focus and resources to Afghanistan. 

Implicitly addressing the intense political debates surrounding the closing of the Guantanamo Bay detention center and the interrogation techniques of the previous administration, Obama argued that maintaining high moral standards enhances, rather than compromises, American strength. 

"We recruit allies. We win the peace. We preserve our moral authority," Obama said. "That is a source of our power. That is why America must always lead."

Beyond traditional battlefields, the President warned the graduates that their careers would be defined by a rapidly shifting security landscape. He cited emerging non-traditional threats, including cyber warfare, piracy, global pandemics, climate change, and the proliferation of nuclear weapons.

Bringing the speech directly to the navy’s recent achievements, Obama drew loud cheers when he referenced the April rescue of Captain Richard Phillips from Somali pirates by Navy SEALs. He held up the operation as an example of the discipline, precision, and courage expected of the new officers. 

"When the world saw those SEALs... they saw the very best of America," Obama said. "They saw the calm, quiet discipline that marks the men and women of our armed forces."

Acknowledging the heavy burden placed on military families after nearly eight years of continuous war, the President pledged to use American military might judiciously. He promised the graduates that he would only send them into harm’s way when absolutely necessary, with clear objectives and the full support of the government.

"I will not send you into harm's way unless it is absolutely necessary, and when I do, I will equip you with the strategy, the equipment, and the support you need to get the job done," he vowed.

Following the address, Obama spent nearly two hours shaking hands and presenting diplomas to every graduating officer. 

As the ceremony concluded with the traditional throwing of the midshipmen’s caps into the air, the newly minted officers prepared to disperse across the globe. For the Class of 2009, the President’s message served as both a charge and a reminder: that as leaders in an unpredictable world, their greatest strength would lie in upholding the ideals of the nation they had sworn to defend.
